The street has a name, but nobody can agree on which.

At the end of it stands a blue house with a yellow door, and the yellow door has a small brass bell that rings only when it is not needed. For forty years, the bell has announced nothing in particular. Rain, perhaps. A visitor. A decision. One of the neighbors, an old woman who waters her geraniums with such precision it looks like a science, says it rings when the town is close to becoming true.

I came here because I had lost something. Not an object. A way of being sure. I wanted to ask the bell why it rang, but the bell, like most useful things, was quiet until I stopped asking.

The house had a porch. The porch had a chair. The chair had a coat on it, though no one was sitting. I sat down. The wind moved through the elms in a way that felt less like weather and more like the house breathing. A cat appeared from behind the hedge, gray as a rumor, and sat at the edge of the path without demanding attention.

Inside, the floorboards made small sounds. The walls were lined with books whose titles had become illegible in some languages. On the table were two cups of tea, both half cold, both still drinkable if you believed in second chances. In the drawer by the window, there was a key, a photograph, and a folded piece of paper with the word *later* written in pencil.

I opened the cup and drank.

It tasted like the last warm hour of a long day.

Outside, the bell rang once.

I did not feel alarm. It felt like a question being handed to me, not a warning. I stood, brushed the chair with my sleeve, and walked to the door. The cat followed for a few paces, then stopped and looked back with the expression of a creature that knows the future but has chosen not to discuss it.

The front door opened onto a hallway, though it was also onto the street, and both made sense. The light inside was blue, like the house. The light outside was the pale green of morning. I picked up the key, the photograph, and the paper.

The photograph showed a street that looked exactly like this street, but the blue house had a red door.

The key was cold.

The word *later* was not a promise. It was an invitation to stop rushing toward a future that had not yet agreed to be real.

I walked down the street. I did not know if I was leaving or arriving. The bell rang again, softly, from behind me. I turned once, not to see the house, but to confirm that the moment had been real.

Then I walked on.

The house remained. The cat remained. The street, perhaps, remembered. And somewhere in the quiet of the morning, the bell let its sound go, because it had finally been heard.
